newsitem.title: USA: Greenpeace dumps coal in front of U.S. Capitol.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace dumps coal in front of U.S. Capitol.

text.p: The environmental group Greenpeace got past security forces on Wednesday and dumped a truckload of coal and seven oil drums in front of the U.S. Capitol.

Greenpeace said the action was taken to protest a resolution introduced by Sen. Robert Byrd, a West Virginia Democrat, that the group said threatened to derail international negotiations on climate change.
It said the resolution would undermine an international agreement signed by the United States to take steps to cut "greenhouse gas emissions" caused by burning coal and oil.

The dump truck was able to get onto a road servicing a congressional parking area generally used by reporters and aides in front of the Capitol and stopped at barriers set about 150 yards from the building.
The truck came down the road the wrong way through an exit-only opening and evaded police on motorcycles who tried to block it, Capitol Police spokesman Sgt. Dan Nichols said.

At a time of heightened awareness about terrorism threats since the Oklahoma City bombing of a federal building, the group's actions were "extremely irresponsible and dangerous," he said. "Their actions put themselves in danger and our officers and the general public, and that's unacceptable."

Byrd's measure says the United States should not sign any agreement related to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change in Kyoto in December if the agreement does not mandate reduction of greenhouse gas emissions for developing countries as well or would result in "serious harm" to the U.S. economy.

"I am on the side of the environment in this fight," Byrd said in a statement. "But if China, India, Mexico, and other developing nations continue to expand their economies in environmentally unsound ways ... the threat to human health and the environment ... will continue to hang over all of us."
The environmental group dumped the very materials it is concerned about but said it would clean up once the 45 senators who signed the Byrd resolution withdrew their names.

The truck driver was charged with assault of a police officer, a felony that carries a fine of up to $5,000 or five years in prison, or both, Nichols said. The driver and three other protesters were also charged with misdemeanors of obstructing traffic on Capitol grounds and demonstrating without a permit, Nichols said.
